core: Definition of overfitting: a model that fits its training data extremely well (too closely, even exactly) but fails to make accurate predictions on new data (IBM)
Core intuition: memorizing the training set versus learning the general pattern, with the original student-who-memorized-the-practice-exam example
Why it happens: a model that is too complex or trains too long can learn the noise (irrelevant details) in the data
Signs of overfitting: excellent training performance paired with poor test performance; held-out test data as the standard check (training-versus-testing referenced only)
Prevention: more clean and relevant data, simpler models, early stopping, checking on held-out data
Overfitting versus underfitting: too much memorization versus too little learning, both failing on new data; the goal is the sweet spot between them
supporting: Generalization as the fundamental goal of machine learning (IBM machine-learning page)
Bias-variance tradeoff framing kept at a conceptual level, no math
Regularization, feature selection, and ensemble methods named as advanced prevention tools (IBM)
Evaluation of AI systems as part of trustworthiness (NIST AI RMF)

claims.claim: Overfitting occurs when a model fits too closely, or even exactly, to its training data, so that it cannot make accurate predictions on any data other than that training data.
Generalization, the translation of strong performance on training data into useful results on new, real-world data, is the fundamental goal of machine learning.
Overfitting happens when a model trains for too long on sample data or is too complex, causing it to learn noise, the irrelevant information, within the dataset.
The telltale sign of overfitting is low error on the training data paired with high error on the test data; setting aside part of the data as a test set is the standard way to check for overfitting.

Standard ways to avoid overfitting include early stopping, training with more clean and relevant data, feature selection to simplify the model, and regularization; more data only helps when it is clean and relevant.

Underfitting occurs when the model has not trained long enough or the input variables are not significant enough to establish the dominant trend; underfitted models also generalize poorly to new data, with high bias and less variance.

Overfitting and underfitting sit on a bias-variance tradeoff, and the goal when fitting a model is the sweet spot in between, where the model establishes the dominant trend and applies it broadly to new data.
Trustworthy design, development, use, and evaluation of AI products, services, and systems includes checking how they perform in the contexts where they will actually be used.

conflictingEvidence.issue: Whether overfitting is best described as memorization, noise-fitting, or a statistical property (high variance).
positions: IBM frames overfitting as fitting too closely to training data and learning noise, with low training error and high variance as indicators.
Popular treatments describe it simply as 'the model memorized the training data'.
Some statistical treatments emphasize variance and the bias-variance tradeoff without the memorization language.
conflictingEvidence.resolution: The lesson uses IBM's framing throughout: memorization of the training set and learning noise are the accessible descriptions, and the bias-variance tradeoff is named conceptually without math, per the LITERACY level.

conflictingEvidence.issue: Whether adding more data reliably prevents overfitting.
positions: IBM: expanding the training set with more data can increase accuracy by offering more chances to parse the dominant relationship, but this works best with clean, relevant data; otherwise the model can just add complexity and overfit.
A common shorthand is 'more data fixes overfitting' with no qualification.
conflictingEvidence.resolution: The lesson follows IBM's qualified version: more clean, relevant data helps; the qualification is stated explicitly in the lesson and in a common-mistakes entry.
